tagline: A former toll road leads from Wilmington into du Pont estate country
intro: From Wilmington’s downtown streets, the Brandywine Valley National Scenic Byway reaches rolling hills and country estates on Routes 52 and 100. Delaware’s transportation department gives this Delaware drive a length of 12.25 miles and a driving time of about an hour. It attributes the byway’s national significance to three centuries of industrial history, including the lower Brandywine’s water-powered mills. On Route 52, the road narrows beyond Greenville to two lanes through woods and open fields.

The Kennett Pike began as a turnpike built between 1811 and 1813 to connect industrial Wilmington with southeastern Pennsylvania. A century later, motorists demanded better roads. Pierre S. du Pont bought the pike in 1919; its toll gates came down, and widening and resurfacing followed. After the work, he sold it to the Delaware State Highway Department for $1. The road became part of Delaware’s scenic highway system in 2002 and a National Scenic Byway in 2005.

Start at Rodney Square and follow Route 52 out through Wilmington and Greenville. Nemours and Hagley are nearby excursions in the Wilmington area. Continue past Winterthur to Centreville and the Pennsylvania line. The Route 100 branch passes Montchanin Village and Brandywine Creek State Park on its own way to the state line.

moments.title: Nemours Estate
moments.text: Nemours translates a French architectural model into a Delaware country estate. Alfred I. du Pont created it in 1909–10 as a gift for his second wife, Alicia. Carrère and Hastings designed the mansion in the Louis XVI style, with 105 rooms on four floors. Inside is a clock made for Marie Antoinette that she never received. The gardens extend the French theme: their design draws on Versailles, with a central axis running a third of a mile from the mansion’s facade. A renovation completed in 2008 repaired furnishings and interior finishes as well as the reflecting pool and formal gardens.
moments.notice: The formal gardens’ central axis extends a third of a mile from the mansion facade.

moments.title: Hagley Museum and Library
moments.text: The Brandywine’s fall supplied power for the black powder mills that Éleuthère Irénée du Pont founded in 1802. He also chose the site for its timber, willow trees for charcoal, nearby shipping and construction stone. The mills closed in 1921; museum planning began in 1952, the company’s 150th anniversary. Hagley’s grounds now include the powder yards, the first du Pont family home and garden in the United States, and a nineteenth-century machine shop. Exhibits also follow the company’s nineteenth-century employees, connecting their changing lives with new machinery and production methods.
moments.notice: The powder yards and nineteenth-century machine shop remain part of the museum grounds.

moments.title: Winterthur
moments.text: Winterthur’s rooms bring together architectural pieces from other American houses. After inheriting the estate in 1927, Henry Francis du Pont and his wife Ruth tripled the manor’s size and fitted it with salvaged interiors. In 1951, he made the mansion a public museum of American decorative arts and moved into a smaller house on the estate. Its 175 period-room displays sit within an estate that also includes naturalistic gardens and old-growth forest. Landscape architect Marian Cruger Coffin helped du Pont design the gardens, whose plantings include rhododendrons, azaleas and dogwood.
moments.notice: Period rooms incorporate architectural elements salvaged from seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century American homes.
